trips.title: Who makes the decisions?
trips.goal: We are learning how people can have a say in local decisions.
trips.invitation: Step inside the place where Surrey makes decisions.
trips.route: Watch selected parts of the tour together. Pause when a room or service gives you a clue about who does what. Keep one question for your civic case wall.

stops.title: A place to decide
stops.notice: Look for the council meeting space or a description of council’s work.
stops.question: What decision might be made here?

stops.title: People doing the work
stops.notice: Notice a city service or department mentioned in the tour.
stops.question: Who turns a council decision into something people can use?

stops.title: A voice that is missing
stops.notice: Think of someone affected by your class’s chosen issue.
stops.question: What would you need to ask them before deciding?

trips.task: Add one decision-maker and one unanswered question to your civic case wall.
trips.entry: Choose a shared-space issue: a park, crossing or recreation centre. Say who might be affected.
trips.extension: Compare the City’s explanation with a community source. What does each help you understand?
trips.check: Can you explain the difference between making a decision and carrying it out?

fallback.title: Who makes the decisions? · text and table-top route
facts: Surrey’s council makes local decisions; city staff carry out the work of city departments.
People affected by a decision may have different needs and different opportunities to be heard.
A City-produced tour explains the institution’s work. It cannot speak for every resident.
fallback.action: Imagine the class is choosing where to put a new reading corner. Name who decides, who sets it up, and whose needs must be heard. Transfer those three roles to your civic issue.

teacher.placement: Social Studies: Civic Decision Brief, Part 2, Build one civic case wall. Use instead of 8–10 minutes of the institution-source overview. Retain the other sources and case wall.
teacher.prepare: Preview a short council/services excerpt. The full video is about 17 minutes; do not add the whole video to this lesson. Board or paper is enough.
teacher.model: Council could decide to fund a park upgrade. Staff would organize the work. We still need to hear from people who use the park.
teacher.misconception: The mayor does not make every decision alone. A promotional tour is one institutional perspective, not proof that everyone has equal influence.
teacher.assessment: Listen for an accurate decision-making role and a relevant missing voice. No new SpacesEDU post is needed.
teacher.curriculum: Social Studies 6: government systems and civic participation; local context supports comparison with other systems.
teacher.sourceNotes: Official City tour page links this video and the student workbook. The fictional class-space activity is our teaching analogy.
teacher.verification: Daryl confirmed direct video access. On 2026-09-05 the browser loaded a 17:02 player, but media time did not advance, so this is not an observed playback pass. No captions were available in that player state. Embedded and school-network playback remain untested.
grades: K–2: use one brief excerpt and discuss a fair choice for a shared space.
Grades 3–5: name who decides and one person to ask.
Grades 6–8: connect authority, evidence and participation.
Grades 9–12: compare formal participation with practical access and accountability.

trips.title: Meet rainforest researchers
trips.goal: We are learning how people respond to an issue and how evidence helps us judge that response.
trips.invitation: What would you ask a scientist working in a forest?
trips.route: Optional viewing: choose the coastal mangrove segment with Angelo Bernardino. Then read our separate case card in the three stops. The card describes a later study; it is not a transcript of the tour.

stops.title: Listen before deciding
stops.notice: Later source, July 2022: Margaret Awuor Owuor and Angelo Bernardino studied how people in Curuça, Brazil used and valued mangrove forests. Their team interviewed about 200 people over 10 days.
stops.question: Who responded, and what did they do?

stops.title: Connect people and place
stops.notice: The article describes community connections with fishing and crab collecting. These interviews document local uses and perspectives.
stops.question: Why might a conservation decision need this kind of evidence?

stops.title: Keep the claim fair
stops.notice: The researchers were still analysing their results when the article was published. It does not report the success of a later conservation policy.
stops.question: What can you say from this source—and what would require more evidence?

trips.task: Make one response record: name the people, explain their action, add a source detail and state a limit. Then return to the other response investigations.
trips.entry: Use four headings: Who / Did what / Source detail / Still unknown. Explain your ideas aloud to a partner first.
trips.extension: Compare this research response with another response to your class issue. What different evidence would you need to judge each?
trips.check: Did you distinguish an action that happened from a successful outcome that has not been shown?

fallback.title: Meet rainforest researchers · text and table-top route
facts: Later source, July 2022: Margaret Awuor Owuor and Angelo Bernardino studied how people in Curuça, Brazil used and valued mangrove forests. Their team interviewed about 200 people over 10 days.
The article describes community connections with fishing and crab collecting. These interviews document local uses and perspectives.
The researchers were still analysing their results when the article was published. It does not report the success of a later conservation policy.
fallback.action: Make one response record: name the people, explain their action, add a source detail and state a limit. Then return to the other response investigations.

teacher.placement: Social Studies: Responses Under Pressure, Part 1. Replace one source station with this prepared mangrove case card. The video supplies optional place/context; the separate July 2022 article supplies the response evidence. Keep the other response investigations.
teacher.prepare: Use the prepared case card even when watching the tour. If you preview and locate the coastal mangrove segment, use 3–5 minutes from it plus the card and discussion within the 10–12 minute station. Exact video timestamps remain unverified.
teacher.model: Owuor and Bernardino asked local people about mangroves. Around 200 interviews show how people use and value the forest. These interviews do not prove that a later conservation policy worked.
teacher.misconception: Scenery alone is not evidence that a conservation action works. Do not treat every place shown as the same Amazon habitat.
teacher.assessment: Look for actor, actual action, source detail and a fair limit. A proposed method alone cannot count as this response record.
teacher.curriculum: Social Studies 6: resources and responses to complex issues; source evaluation. Ecosystem detail is enrichment rather than a replacement for Grade 6 science systems.
teacher.sourceNotes: The April 2022 video description identifies the researchers and places. The prepared case card paraphrases a separate National Geographic article first published August 31, 2022 about July 2022 interviews. The later study is not claimed to appear in the video.

trips.title: A building that borrows from nature
trips.goal: We are learning how shapes, light and colour can change a space.
trips.invitation: Could a room feel like being inside a shell?
trips.route: Meet architect Antoni Gaudí and the craftspeople who shaped Casa Batlló in Barcelona. Use the official illustrated interior guide for three features below. In the 360° video, look for them if visible; its imaginative effects belong to the modern production.

stops.title: Lobby · a curve
stops.notice: The interior guide shows a curved wooden stair handrail that resembles an animal’s spine.
stops.question: How could a handrail be both useful and expressive?

stops.title: Attic · repeated arches
stops.notice: The guide shows a row of arches that suggests ribs.
stops.question: How does repetition affect where your eyes travel?

stops.title: Lightwell · colour and light
stops.notice: Tiles are darker blue above and paler below. Lower windows are larger to admit light.
stops.question: How does this design combine appearance and practical use?

trips.task: Sketch a reading corner or entrance using one nature-inspired shape. Label what the feature helps people do.
trips.entry: Start with the outline of a leaf or shell. Turn one part into a seat, shade or doorway.
trips.extension: Suggest a way to test whether your design is comfortable and useful.
trips.check: Can you explain both an artistic choice and its possible effect on an audience?

fallback.title: A building that borrows from nature · text and table-top route
facts: Antoni Gaudí redesigned an existing Barcelona house with craftspeople working in wood, glass, iron, ceramics and stone.
The lobby has a curved wooden handrail; the attic repeats arch shapes.
The lightwell uses darker tiles above and paler tiles below; lower windows are larger to admit light.
These are architectural features. The modern video’s imaginative effects are not Gaudí’s building materials.
fallback.action: Observe a leaf, or draw a simple curved line. Use the shape in an original reading-corner sketch. Label a purpose, then ask a partner what they would test.

teacher.placement: Arts: Pattern, Motion, Light & Environment. Replace one opening mentor encounter in Meet the artists / Look. Keep the artist-response card and original art-making.
teacher.prepare: Open the illustrated interior guide and locate Lobby, Attic and Lightwell. These are verified building features, not verified video timestamps. Use the video as an optional first encounter, then retain the existing artist-response card and making.
teacher.model: Gaudí repeats curved arches in the attic. The pattern reminds me of ribs. I could repeat curved supports in a reading corner to create a sheltered feeling.
teacher.misconception: A nature-inspired form is an interpretation, not proof that the architect copied a particular plant. Do not measure real dimensions from the video.
teacher.assessment: Look for a named artistic choice and an explained audience effect; students may speak, sketch or label.
teacher.curriculum: Arts Education 6: elements and principles, exploring creative works, creating and communicating. ADST connection: purpose and user needs.
teacher.sourceNotes: Official Casa Batlló page supplies this English 360° video and desktop navigation instructions. Treat imaginative presentation as part of the produced experience.

trips.title: Swim along with a sea turtle
trips.goal: We are learning to use precise observations in our writing.
trips.invitation: What changes when the camera travels with a turtle?
trips.route: Watch a short section. Pause on one clear frame, then another after the camera has moved. Gather exact words before imagining a story.

stops.title: Describe one frame
stops.notice: Name a visible colour, shape, texture or movement.
stops.question: Which word is most precise?

stops.title: Change the viewpoint
stops.notice: Compare what becomes visible after the camera moves.
stops.question: What can you see now that you could not see before?

stops.title: Separate seeing from guessing
stops.notice: Choose one observation and one imagined idea.
stops.question: Which could a classmate check in the footage?

trips.task: Gather five precise words and use two in a short poem. Mark an invented thought as imagination.
trips.entry: Say two observations to a partner, or sketch one frame and label it.
trips.extension: Rewrite one line from a different camera position. Explain what changed.
trips.check: Can you point to evidence for an observation and identify an imaginative detail?

fallback.title: Swim along with a sea turtle · text and table-top route
facts: This WWF footage comes from a camera carried by a turtle. It follows the camera’s position.
The camera does not show exactly what the turtle’s eyes see or what it thinks.
A poem can include imagination, but we should not present an invented animal thought as a scientific finding.
fallback.action: Place a pencil case on a desk. Observe it from above and from seated desk height. Collect five precise words. Write two lines; label any imagined voice as fiction.

teacher.placement: Language Arts: Precision poetry studio, Observe exactly / Look. Replace the generic observation source with this short encounter; retain drafting and revision.
teacher.prepare: Preview two clear frames. Plan 2–3 minutes of footage and 4–5 minutes for words and talk. An actual desk object supports the backup.
teacher.model: “The view tilts and the reef passes below” is an observation if visible. “I am searching for a friend” is an invented turtle voice.
teacher.misconception: An animal-mounted camera is not a model of animal vision or a source of animal-care advice.
teacher.assessment: Listen for precise vocabulary and separation of observation from invention. Keep the existing poem assessment.
teacher.curriculum: English Language Arts 6: sensory detail, creative language and distinguishing evidence from inference. Animal ecology is enrichment.
teacher.sourceNotes: The WWF-Australia video is corroborated by its official channel playlist. No exact timestamps or biological sensory claims are assumed.
teacher.verification: Source reviewed 2026-09-05. Player or source metadata checked; sustained video playback, lesson embed and school-projector use still need confirmation. Use the prepared text route if video cannot play.
grades: K–2: notice two visible things without guessing feelings.
Grades 6–8: explain the limit of camera evidence.
Grades 9–12: discuss how recording tools shape evidence.

trips.title: Travel inside a kidney
trips.goal: We are learning how kidneys remove waste while keeping what the body needs.
trips.invitation: How does your body avoid throwing away useful materials?
trips.route: Watch the short video from 0:00 to 3:55, then discuss the three stops below. Replay relevant moments as needed.

stops.title: Blood arrives
stops.notice: Look for the route bringing blood into the kidney.
stops.question: Why does blood need to pass through the kidneys?

stops.title: Keep and remove
stops.notice: Notice that filtering is followed by keeping or returning useful materials.
stops.question: Why would removing everything be a problem?

stops.title: Two different routes
stops.notice: Follow blood returning to the body and urine travelling towards the bladder.
stops.question: What does each route carry?

trips.task: Draw two outgoing arrows from a kidney: blood back to the body, and urine towards the bladder. Explain one difference.
trips.entry: Use these labels: blood, kidney, urine, bladder. Trace the routes with a finger and explain aloud.
trips.extension: Connect the kidney’s job to the lesson’s hot-day case. Explain why the body needs to adjust how much water it keeps.
trips.check: Are blood and urine shown on different outgoing routes?

fallback.title: Travel inside a kidney · text and table-top route
facts: Blood brings dissolved wastes and other substances to the kidneys.
Kidneys filter blood and return needed materials, including much of the water, to the blood.
Urine carries wastes and extra water along the ureters to the bladder. Blood returns through blood vessels.
fallback.action: Sketch a kidney between an incoming blood arrow and two outgoing routes. Label the outgoing routes “blood to body” and “urine to bladder.” Explain why the useful materials cannot all be discarded.

teacher.placement: Science: Case file: too hot, too thirsty, Part 3, Keep, return, or remove? Replace the kidney-video overview. Keep the three decisions, urinary route and feedback explanation.
teacher.prepare: Use the whole 0:00–3:55 video, then the three discussion stops. Internal pause timestamps have not been verified. About 3:55 of video plus pauses and a 3-minute model. Preteach kidney, waste and urine. Skip detailed nephron and hormone vocabulary as required recall.
teacher.model: Blood returns to the body carrying materials it still needs. Urine carries wastes and extra water towards the bladder on a different route.
teacher.misconception: Urine is not simply a drink passing straight through. Blood and urine do not share the same outgoing tube.
teacher.assessment: Check the two distinct routes and the explanation of why useful materials are kept.
teacher.curriculum: BC Science 6: excretory system, structures and functions, connections between body systems.
teacher.sourceNotes: Official TED-Ed page embeds the same video. YouTube metadata identifies TED-Ed, about 3:55, English captions and permitted embedding. Metadata is not an observed playback pass.

trips.title: Make a home in orbit
trips.goal: We are learning how a design can solve a problem in an extreme environment.
trips.invitation: How would you sleep or wash if you kept floating?
trips.route: Look inside the sleeping and hygiene areas with astronaut Suni Williams. Suggested clips: 0:36–2:25 and 3:05–4:40. Discuss the three stops, then choose one useful design feature.

stops.title: Somewhere to sleep
stops.notice: Find a feature that keeps a sleeping person in place.
stops.question: What problem does that feature solve?

stops.title: An everyday job
stops.notice: Notice one way washing or storing objects differs from home.
stops.question: Why might an everyday object need a different design?

stops.title: Choose an explanation
stops.notice: Choose one feature to explain in your own exhibit.
stops.question: What can the video show, and what needs a second source?

trips.task: Sketch a useful feature for a room in space. Label the problem, the feature and one question you would test.
trips.entry: Choose a sleeping-bag anchor, handhold or storage strap. Explain what it keeps in place.
trips.extension: Compare your feature with a useful design on Earth. Which problem changes in orbit?
trips.check: Does your explanation connect a design feature to a specific problem?

fallback.title: Make a home in orbit · text and table-top route
facts: In orbit, the space station and its occupants are falling around Earth together. Gravity has not disappeared.
A secured sleeping bag can stop a sleeping astronaut from drifting around the room.
Handholds and storage restraints help people move and keep objects in place.
fallback.action: Draw a small room. Add a secured sleeping bag, a handhold and a storage strap. Label the problem each solves, then choose one feature for your exhibit.

teacher.placement: Science: Cosmic Exhibit Studio, Part 2, Choose one story worth teaching. This is an alternative to the Mars visit, not an extra task. Replace 10–12 minutes of broad source browsing; keep the two-source exhibit plan.
teacher.prepare: Suggested clips: 0:36–2:25 (sleep) and 3:05–4:40 (toothbrush), 3:24 total viewing. These are YouTube automatic chapter markers, not NASA-authored transcript timestamps; preview before teaching. Allow the rest of the 10–12 minutes for discussion and design.
teacher.model: A sleeping bag attached to the wall stops the astronaut drifting while asleep. It would not need the same restraint in a bedroom on Earth.
teacher.misconception: Floating in orbit does not mean there is no gravity. The 2012 footage is not a report about today’s crew.
teacher.assessment: Look for problem → feature → explanation, plus one limit or follow-up question.
teacher.curriculum: Science 6: extreme environments and exploration; ADST design connections. Newton’s laws are a possible later extension, not the core claim of this room tour.
teacher.sourceNotes: NASA’s official Suni ISS Tour page embeds this archival NASA Johnson video. English automatic captions and permitted embedding found in player metadata.

trips.title: Stand on Mars with a rover
trips.goal: We are learning what a robot’s camera can tell us about another world.
trips.invitation: Where would you ask a rover to investigate next?
trips.route: Watch the short video from 0:00 to 3:01, then discuss the three stops below. Replay relevant moments as needed.

stops.title: Find the camera’s position
stops.notice: Look for part of the rover and the surrounding ground.
stops.question: What can this camera position reveal or hide?

stops.title: Compare rock features
stops.notice: Look for two rock surfaces or layers that differ.
stops.question: What can you describe without guessing how they formed?

stops.title: Ask the next question
stops.notice: Listen to the scientist’s explanation of the ancient environment.
stops.question: What other evidence would help test that explanation?

trips.task: Choose one feature. Say “I can see…” and “To find out more, I would need…”. Use it to narrow your exhibit question.
trips.entry: Choose shape, texture or layers. Sketch one contrast and ask a question.
trips.extension: Compare natural-colour and enhanced-colour images on NASA’s source page. Why might a scientist use both?
trips.check: Did you distinguish an observation from an explanation that needs more evidence?

fallback.title: Stand on Mars with a rover · text and table-top route
facts: A rover panorama combines camera images to show a wide view of the landscape.
NASA uses enhanced colour in this view to make differences easier to see. It is not exactly how the scene would appear to human eyes there.
Rock shapes and layers give scientists clues; a picture alone does not prove that life existed.
fallback.action: Draw two imaginary rock layers: a smooth lower layer and a pebbly upper layer. Label this “our model, not a Mars photograph.” Name an observation, propose two explanations and say what evidence would help choose between them.

teacher.placement: Science: Cosmic Exhibit Studio, Part 2. Choose this OR Make a home in orbit as a bounded source encounter. Keep the two-source requirement and later model-making.
teacher.prepare: Use the whole 0:00–3:01 video, then the three discussion stops. Internal pause timestamps have not been verified. The NASA guided video is about 3:01. Allow 1 minute to locate Mars, 3 minutes to view and 4–6 minutes for three pauses and the exhibit question.
teacher.model: I can see contrasting layers. I would need more information about the rocks before explaining how the layers formed.
teacher.misconception: Enhanced colour is a scientific display choice. A rover view is not proof of past life or a scale drawing for measuring distances.
teacher.assessment: Check that the student can name an observation, a question and an evidence source that might answer it.
teacher.curriculum: BC Science 6: solar-system environments, space exploration, evidence and model limitations.
teacher.sourceNotes: NASA’s panorama page provides the source image, enhanced-colour explanation and narrated video. NASA JPL YouTube metadata lists the guided video, English captions and permitted embedding.

trips.title: Meet the people protecting an island
trips.goal: We are learning how different people and skills contribute to one project.
trips.invitation: Who helps protect a place that most classrooms cannot visit?
trips.route: Open the original tour in a new tab. Use its thumbnail strip to select Stops 5, 8 and 12. Drag gently to look around and open the information points. Return here between stops.

stops.title: Listen for birds · tour Stop 5
stops.notice: Look for the sound-recording tool described at the western side of the island.
stops.question: What skill would someone need to turn recordings into useful evidence?

stops.title: Watch without standing there · tour Stop 8
stops.notice: Find the wildlife-camera information at Naupaka, the eastern tip.
stops.question: What can a camera record while people are elsewhere?

stops.title: Meet the team · tour Stop 12
stops.notice: Open the career information inside the weatherport.
stops.question: Name one role and a contribution described by the person doing it.

trips.task: Add one role, one tool and one skill to your career map. Mark one learning-pathway question that the source does not answer.
trips.entry: Choose sound recorder or camera. Say what a person would do with the information it collects.
trips.extension: Use tour Stop 6 to investigate how another part of the project connects with monitoring.
trips.check: Is the contribution supported by the source? Did you avoid guessing a person’s qualifications?

fallback.title: Meet the people protecting an island · text and table-top route
facts: The Kauaʻi Endangered Seabird Recovery Project works with partners to protect seabirds and their habitat on Lehua.
The provider’s guide describes sound monitoring at Stop 5 and wildlife cameras at Stop 8.
Technology collects evidence; people still need to interpret it and decide what to do.
fallback.action: Choose a sound recorder or camera for observing a fictional school garden. Sketch the tool, name one skill needed to use its evidence, and add another person whose work connects. Label the garden plan as your proposal.

teacher.placement: Career Education: The people and skills behind one project, Study pathways / Look. Replace 10–12 minutes of the existing profile investigation, retaining the other profiles and career map.
teacher.prepare: Open Stops 5, 8 and 12 before class. Turn off automatic rotation using the tour’s pause control if needed. Project the browser; students do not need headsets or accounts.
teacher.model: A recording tool can collect bird calls when nobody is nearby. Someone needs to identify and interpret those calls. A camera can add another kind of evidence.
teacher.misconception: Equipment does not make decisions by itself. Do not guess qualifications or turn the project into a generic Hawaiian or Indigenous voice.
teacher.assessment: Look for role → skill → contribution and an honest unanswered pathway question.
teacher.curriculum: Career Education 6: learning about work and pathways, skills and contributions to community; science inquiry enrichment.
